cards.front: Pump and dump
cards.back: A manipulative scheme in which fraudsters accumulate shares at low prices, spread false or misleading positive rumors to inflate (pump) the stock price, then sell (dump) their shares at the inflated price, leaving other investors with losses.

cards.front: Front running
cards.back: Placing an order for one's own account ahead of a known pending customer order in order to profit from the anticipated price movement. Prohibited.

cards.front: A mutual fund places a market order with your firm to buy 300,000 shares of AABB. Before entering the order to the market, an RR aware of the order enters a buy for 500 shares in his own account. What violation is this?
cards.back: Front running — placing a personal order ahead of a known customer order to benefit from the anticipated price impact. Prohibited.

cards.front: Churning (excessive trading)
cards.back: Trading excessively in a customer's account—in frequency or size inconsistent with the client's objectives, history, or financial ability—to generate commissions. It is a breach of fiduciary duty and is prohibited.

cards.front: What two manipulative practices involve entering or falsely reporting trades to influence a stock's price at the start or end of the trading day?
cards.back: Marking the open (manipulating the opening price) and marking the close (manipulating the closing price, often to boost portfolio valuations). Both are prohibited.

cards.front: Freeriding (cash account violation)
cards.back: Buying securities and selling them before paying for the purchase. Prohibited in both cash and margin accounts. Penalty: the account is frozen for 90 days, during which purchases require cash or marginable securities on deposit before the trade.

cards.front: Matching orders (painting the tape)
cards.back: Two parties arrange to buy and sell the same security to each other at substantially the same price to create the false appearance of trading volume/activity. Prohibited.

cards.front: Are any securities exempt from the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws?
cards.back: No. No security is exempt from the antifraud provisions. Fraud and market manipulation are prohibited in the trading of any security.

cards.front: Is merely possessing material nonpublic information illegal?
cards.back: No. Possession of inside information is not illegal. It is the use of that information to trade for gain or to avoid a loss—or communicating it to others who trade—that constitutes insider trading.

cards.front: Inside (material nonpublic) information
cards.back: Any material information about a company that has not been disseminated to, or is not readily available to, the general public, and that would likely influence the price of the company's stock.

cards.front: Under the Insider Trading Act, who can be held liable in an insider trading case?
cards.back: Both the tipper (who passes the information) and the tippee (who receives and trades on it), as well as anyone who trades on information they knew or should have known was nonpublic, and any controlling person.

cards.front: What is a firewall (information barrier)?
cards.back: Written policies and procedures a BD must establish to restrict the flow of material nonpublic information between departments of the firm in order to prevent the misuse of inside information.

cards.front: What are the civil and criminal penalties for an individual who violates insider trading rules?
cards.back: Civil penalty: up to 3 times the profit gained or loss avoided (treble damages). Criminal penalty: up to $5 million in fines and up to 20 years in prison.

cards.front: What is the maximum penalty a BD may face if its employee commits insider trading?
cards.back: The firm can be fined the greater of 3 times the damages or $25 million. A controlling person can be fined the greater of $1 million or 3 times the profit/loss avoided.

cards.front: Contemporaneous traders
cards.back: Persons who trade on the opposite side of the market in the same security at or near the same time as someone trading on inside information. They have a private right of action against the violator and may sue up to 5 years after the violation.

cards.front: Under Dodd-Frank, what bounty may an informant receive for providing original information about an insider trading or securities law violation?
cards.back: 10% to 30% of the amount recovered by the SEC, based on the value of the information provided.

cards.front: What is the purpose of FINRA Rule 5130?
cards.back: To protect the integrity of the public offering process by ensuring members make bona fide public offerings at the POP, do not withhold IPO shares for their own benefit, and do not allow industry insiders to gain access to new issues at the expense of public customers.

cards.front: List the categories of restricted persons under FINRA Rule 5130 (those prohibited from buying common stock IPOs at the POP).
cards.back: 1) Member firms; 2) employees of member firms; 3) finders and fiduciaries to the managing underwriter (attorneys, accountants, financial consultants); 4) portfolio managers (anyone with authority to buy/sell securities for a bank, S&L, insurer, or investment company); 5) any person owning 10% or more of a member firm; and 6) immediate family members of the above.

cards.front: Who qualifies as 'immediate family' for purposes of Rule 5130 restricted persons?
cards.back: Parents, in-laws, spouse, siblings, children, and any other person who is materially supported by the restricted person. Aunts, uncles, and grandparents are NOT immediate family unless they share the household with a restricted person.

cards.front: Jim is a restricted person under Rule 5130. Of the following relatives, who may purchase a new common stock issue at the POP: Jim's brother, grandfather, sister, or daughter?
cards.back: Jim's grandfather. Grandparents are not considered immediate family under Rule 5130 (unless they share a household with the restricted person). Siblings and children are immediate family and are restricted.

cards.front: What is the de minimis exemption under Rule 5130?
cards.back: An account may purchase a new equity issue at the POP if restricted persons' beneficial ownership of the account does not exceed 10% in total.

cards.front: Daryl (a restricted person) owns 5% of an investment club's account. His brother Larry (also restricted) then buys in for an additional 6%, bringing the brothers' combined ownership to 11%. May the club purchase a new IPO at the POP?
cards.back: No. Once restricted persons' combined beneficial ownership exceeds 10% (here, 11%), the de minimis exemption is lost and the account may no longer purchase the IPO at the POP.

cards.front: Before selling an IPO to an account, what must the representative obtain from the account owner?
cards.back: A written representation from the account owner(s) that the account is eligible to purchase the new common stock issue at the POP (i.e., is not beneficially owned by restricted persons beyond the de minimis threshold).

cards.front: Four questions used to determine if tipper/tippee insider trading liability exists?
cards.back: 1) Is the information material and nonpublic? 2) Does the tipper owe a fiduciary duty to a company or its shareholders? 3) Does the tipper meet the personal benefits test (gaining something, even reputational)? 4) Did the tippee know, or should they have known, the information was confidential/nonpublic?
